extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and trademark practitioners who represent clients before the USPTO (including sponsoring attorneys and support staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and requirements for trademark practitioners' conduct before the USPTO, including signature rules, USPTO.gov account responsibilities, supervisory duties for non-practitioner assistants, certification obligations when presenting papers, and related remedial/monitoring sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. Counsel Rule (37 C.F.R. § 2.11(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign-domiciled trademark applicants or registrants must be represented before the USPTO by an attorney who is licensed to practice law in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy objectives: increase compliance with U.S. trademark law and USPTO regulations, improve accuracy of submissions, and safeguard integrity of the U.S. trademark register (see 84 Fed. Reg. 31498). Practitioners representing foreign-domiciled clients are expected to know and follow the U.S. Counsel Rule and related TMEP guidance (e.g., TMEP §601).

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO.gov account general responsibilities (Trademark Account Agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A USPTO.gov account holder must not permit others to use the trademark-verified USPTO.gov account login credentials, must take reasonable steps to prevent others from learning such account login information, and must promptly notify the USPTO if the holder becomes aware that his or her login credentials have been used by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account holders agree the account will not be used in connection with unauthorized practice of law. Each login requires certifying acceptance of Terms of Use. The Agreement also states one individual may only use one trademark-verified USPTO.gov account and will not request additional accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sponsoring attorney responsibilities for sponsored USPTO.gov accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: An attorney who sponsors a USPTO.gov account is personally, professionally, and ethically responsible for the conduct of each attorney support staff when using a sponsored USPTO.gov account and must take reasonable steps to ensure sponsored staff are familiar with the Agreement and relevant laws, regulations, and USPTO policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable steps include prompt removal of sponsorship when appropriate (e.g., no longer under employment/supervision), immediately removing sponsorship and reporting to USPTO when there is reason to believe an assistant abused or misused a USPTO system (including knowingly submitting false statements or signatures), and ensuring sponsored staff's access/use is consistent with assigned tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark electronic signature rules (37 C.F.R. § 2.193(a),(c); 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: All signatures must be personally entered by the named signatory; an electronic signatory must personally enter any combination of letters, numbers, spaces, and/or punctuation marks adopted as a signature, placed between two forward slash ("/") symbols in the signature block on the electronic submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person may not delegate their authority to sign, and no person may sign or enter the name of another. Typing the electronic signature of another person is not a valid signature; using document-signing software to create or generate another person's electronic signature is likewise improper. See TMEP §611.01 for additional detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature rules are substantive (not technical) and may affect validity
rubrics_metrics.description: The trademark signature rule requiring the named signatory to enter his or her signature on a trademark document is a substantive rule, not a mere 'technical' one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A signature that does not meet the 'personally signed' or 'personally entered' requirements may jeopardize the validity of an application or registration (37 C.F.R. § 2.193(f)). A failure to personally enter a signature—even without wrongful intent—can be a misrepresentation under 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c) and potentially adversely affect applicants' rights and the integrity of the USPTO registration process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certifications when presenting papers (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner presenting any paper to the USPTO certifies that statements of his or her own knowledge are true, and statements made on information and belief are believed to be true; and that, after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances: (i) the paper is not presented for any improper purpose; (ii) legal contentions are warranted by existing law or by a nonfrivolous argument; (iii) factual allegations have evidentiary support or are likely to after investigation; and (iv) denials are warranted on the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting a document with false, misleading, fictitious, or fraudulent information violates 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(1). Presenting papers without reasonable inquiry or to circumvent Rules/Terms of Use constitutes an improper purpose and violates 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(2). Violations may jeopardize the probative value of the filing and can expose the signer to criminal penalties under 18 U.S.C. § 1001 and disciplinary sanctions under 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence obligation (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must provide competent representation to a client, which includes taking reasonable steps to ensure trademark documents are signed in accordance with USPTO trademark signature rules and properly supervising non-practitioner assistants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to take reasonable steps (e.g., monitoring assistants, reviewing filing receipts) may constitute a violation of competence and lead to discipline. Competence implicates familiarity with applicable rules and TMEP guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence obligation (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must act with reasonable diligence in representing clients, including ensuring documents are properly signed, monitoring sponsored assistants, and reviewing filings and filing receipts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not taking reasonable steps to detect or prevent improperly signed submissions (or failing to review filing receipts that would have alerted the practitioner) can violate the duty of diligence and be disciplinary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibilities regarding non-practitioner assistants (37 C.F.R. § 11.503(a)-(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who employs, retains, or sponsors non-practitioner assistants has responsibilities to monitor and supervise those assistants; inadequate monitoring that results in assistants improperly entering a practitioner's signature can violate § 11.503.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sponsoring attorneys must ensure sponsored assistants' access/use is consistent with assigned tasks, remove sponsorship when appropriate, and take prompt corrective action and reporting if misuse occurs. Inadequate monitoring that leads to violations of trademark signature rules is actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misconduct: dishonesty, fraud, deceit, misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting trademark documents to the USPTO that were improperly signed by others (i.e., not personally entered by the named signatory) constitutes conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation under § 11.804(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such presentations may be the predicate for disciplinary sanctions and can undermine the reliability of filings; the practitioner may be sanctioned even if there was no intentional wrongdoing if the practitioner failed to take reasonable steps to prevent or detect the misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misconduct: conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct that undermines the integrity of the USPTO trademark registration process—such as not taking reasonable steps to ensure proper signing, inadequately supervising assistants, presenting improperly signed documents, or failing to verify signatures after receiving filing receipts—constitutes conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice under § 11.804(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include failing to verify signatures in response to filing receipts and thereby allowing improperly signed filings to stand; such conduct can result in public reprimand, probation, suspension, or other discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to review filing receipts and to monitor filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must review filing receipts (and attached documents) and monitor filings that list them as attorney of record to detect unauthorized filings or improper signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to review filing receipts or otherwise monitor filings can result in delayed detection of misuse of sponsored accounts or improperly signed documents and can be a basis for discipline. The Final Order requires bi-weekly searches (see monitoring criterion) and reporting if filings were made without the practitioner's knowledge or consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring procedure required (bi-weekly USPTO search and reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a condition of probation, the respondent must (1) at least bi-weekly search the USPTO's online trademark search system for trademark applications identifying him as attorney of record using the search phrase format AT: firstname AND AT: lastname AND FD: [YYYYMMDD TO YYYYMMDD]; and (2) promptly inform in writing the USPTO Office of Trademark Examination Policy of each trademark document identifying him as attorney of record that was filed without his knowledge or consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additionally, the respondent must, at least every two months, submit a written report to the OED Director confirming completion of the bi-weekly searches and either stating no unexpected filings were found or providing copies of correspondence sent to the Office of Trademark Examination Policy identifying unauthorized filings. This monitoring/reporting regimen is an explicit remedial metric imposed as a sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial training requirement (USPTO Trademark Basics Boot Camp)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a condition of probation, the respondent must enroll in, virtually attend, and complete each of the eight modules comprising the USPTO's Trademark Basics Boot Camp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The respondent must provide a written declaration, affidavit, or statement (28 U.S.C. § 1746) confirming completion prior to termination of probation. Training is presented as a corrective measure to ensure future compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of false or fraudulent statements (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(1); 18 U.S.C. §1001)
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting a document that includes false, misleading, fictitious, or fraudulent information or representations violates 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(1) and may subject the signer to criminal penalties under 18 U.S.C. § 1001.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include false domicile information, attorney information, signatory information (e.g., named signatory did not personally enter signature), applicant information, or false claims of use. Such submissions may also violate § 11.18(b)(2) if presented without reasonable inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions and enforcement mechanisms (public reprimand, probation, suspension process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary remedies can include public reprimand, probation for a specified period, and suspension (up to six months) following an Order to Show Cause if probation conditions are breached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The OED Director may issue an Order to Show Cause and, after notice and an opportunity to respond, request the USPTO Director to immediately suspend a practitioner for up to six months. The OED may also seek discrete discipline for misconduct forming the basis for an Order to Show Cause. The Final Order may be published in the OED FOIA Reading Room and the Official Gazette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation to know and use USPTO/TMEP resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners who represent applicants, registrants, or others before the USPTO in trademark matters are reasonably expected to know the applicable trademark prosecution rules, relevant provisions of the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct, and the potential disciplinary consequences for violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO publishes guidance (e.g., TMEP, USPTO trademark webpages, OED FOIA pages) that practitioners are expected to consult; TMEP §611.01 is cited as providing clear guidance on signature rules and related prohibitions (no signing by paralegals, no document-signing software for others' signatures). Failure to consult or follow published guidance does not excuse noncompliance.
